title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — velle & nolle; materialiter/formaliter
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. Both propositions are false; the Major indeed; for one and the same man can at the same time, for diverse reasons, will and not-will the same thing. And that happens frequently: thence hesitation, and deliberation, and sometimes a fight among our thoughts and volitions. Next there is a will conformed to right reason, and there is an erring will and one that fights right reason: this sometimes fights with itself. Finally no one wills evil as evil formally, that is, insofar as it is privation of a good. And so it ought not seem strange if Adam did not formally will the privation of justice. For so he would have willed his sin under the aspect of evil. What he also says in the Minor, that Adam willed to violate God's precept, materialiter only (so to speak), not formaliter, is true. For he willed that which was a violation of God's precept, but not under the aspect of violation of the divine precept, but under the aspect of some great goodness falsely appearing to him. But if he formally willed to violate God's precept, and yet was unwilling to lose his justice, he was a fool, thinking those things could be separated which in no way could be separated.
pass_b_english: Placeus. Both premises fail. On the major: one and the same person can, for different reasons, will and refuse the same thing at once—hence hesitation, deliberation, and the clash among our thoughts and choices. There is a will aligned with right reason and a will that errs against it; the erring will sometimes fights itself. No one formally wills evil as evil—as privation of a good—so it is no wonder Adam did not formally will the loss of righteousness; that would have been to will his sin under the aspect of evil.

What Garissoles says in the minor—that Adam willed to break the precept only materialiter, not formaliter—is right. Adam willed what was in fact a breach of God's command, but under the guise of some great apparent good, not under the aspect "breach of divine law." If he had formally meant to break the precept and yet refused to lose righteousness, he would have been a fool, imagining inseparable things could be parted.
source_text: PLAC. Utraque propositio est falsa; Major quidem; potest enim unum idemque homo idem eodem tempore ob diversas rationes velle & nolle. Idque evenit frequenter: inde haesitatio, & deliberatio, & pugna nonnunquam inter cogitationes volitionesque nostras. Deinde est voluntas rectae rationi conformis, & est voluntas errans & rectae rationi repugnans: haec secum ipsa nonnunquam pugnat. Denique nemo vult malum qua malum formaliter, hoc est, quatenus est privatio boni. Itaque mirum videri non debet, si Adamus privationem justitiae formaliter non voluit. Ita enim peccatum suum voluisset sub ratione mali. Quod etiam in Minore ait, Adamum voluisse violare Dei praeceptum, materialiter tantum ut sic loquar, non formaliter, verum est. Voluit enim id quod erat violatio praecepti Dei, sed non sub ratione violationis praecepti divini, sed sub ratione magnae cujusdam bonitatis sibi falso apparentis. Quod si formaliter volebat violare Dei praeceptum, & tamen nolebat justitiam suam amittere, stultus erat, putans separari posse, quae separari nullo modo poterant.
